question: Article 3(1)(b) of Directive (EU) 2022/2561, read together with Article 8 and Annex I, Section 4, requires periodic certificate of professional competence (CPC) training for drivers within its scope, consisting of 35 hours every five years1.

In Sweden, Transportstyrelsen, the Swedish Transport Agency, states that a CPC (Yrkeskompetensbevis) is valid for five years and that its renewal requires 35 hours of continuing training2. Compliance with the recurring training requirement entails mandatory time away from work, course attendance and associated administrative requirements.

Questions have been raised as to whether these obligations remain proportionate, particularly for experienced drivers. In the light of the EU’s objectives on road safety, competitiveness, better regulation and addressing the driver shortage: 1.
What evidence does the Commission have on the road-safety impact and costeffectiveness of the 35-hour periodic training requirement every five years?

Will the Commission evaluate whether more proportionate alternatives could be allowed, including risk-based or needs-based training, greater use of digital training, practical assessment, or exemptions for drivers with long experience and a clean safety record?
What flexibility do Member States currently have to reduce the burden while maintaining road-safety standards?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) Well-trained drivers are generally safer drivers, and there is a clear link between the education and training of drivers and road safety1. However, the qualification and training of bus and lorry drivers is not only intended to improve road safety but also the safety of the driver, including during operations carried out by the driver while the vehicle is stopped.

Moreover, it enables the driver to meet the demands of the road transport market. The periodic training is intended to assist drivers in remaining up to date in the skills and knowledge of matters which are essential for their profession. The requirement of 35 hours of periodic training every five years, i.e.

on average one seven-hour period per year, does not appear disproportionate in a professional environment that is rapidly evolving. The periodic training should be relevant for the driver and take his or her specific training needs into account. Experienced drivers should also be able to benefit from it. Member States have several ways to reduce the burden on drivers.

A third of periodic training (up to 12 hours) can already today be given as e-learning, i.e. in a digital way. Moreover, Member States may include the completed specific training as required under other Union legislation for up to one (in exceptional cases two) of the stipulated seven-hour periods2.

The Commission plans to hold an implementation dialogue in November 2026 to discuss any difficulties encountered in the implementation of Directive (EU) 2022/25613, in particular as regards the diverging needs of drivers, and any possibilities of simplification of the training framework.
